R03-G-01: It is often said that the orderly queue reveals something about a people's character, as if patience were a national trait passed down with the language. The explanation is flattering to those who queue well and insulting to those who do not, and it is mostly wrong. A queue is better understood as a small institution: a shared rule, first come first served, enforced by no official and sustained by people who mostly do not know one another and will never meet again. What needs explaining, therefore, is not why some nations are supposedly virtuous but why such a rule, lacking any formal sanction, holds at all among strangers. Part of the answer is that the queue makes its own rule visible. Everyone can see the line, everyone can see their place in it, and anyone who pushes in is caught in the act before an audience that has every reason to object. The penalty is rarely more than a sharp word or a collective stare, yet it is usually enough, because the offender cannot pretend not to know the rule. Compare a crowd waiting at the doors of a bus, where no line has formed. Here the same people who would wait patiently at a ticket counter will often jostle, not because they have become selfish but because no one can say with confidence who arrived first. Without a visible order there is nothing to defend and no clear offence to resent. This suggests that the strength of an informal norm depends less on the virtue of those who follow it than on how legible it makes compliance and violation. Managers of busy offices seem to have grasped this when they introduced numbered tickets: the ticket does not change anyone's character, but it turns an ambiguous crowd into an order that each person can check. Railings, painted footprints and single winding lines that feed many counters work in the same way. The same logic explains why a queue that winds around a corner, so that newcomers cannot tell where it ends, tends to generate precisely the disputes that a visible line prevents. Such devices are inexpensive, and they succeed by removing doubt rather than by threatening punishment. None of this means that the queue is the fairest possible way to allocate a scarce service. It rewards those with time to spare and ignores urgency; a hospital that treated patients strictly in order of arrival would be orderly and indefensible. Nor should the absence of lines be read as disorder, since a crowd may follow subtler conventions that an outsider fails to notice. The point is narrower. Where people do accept first come first served, the rule survives among strangers because it can be seen, and it falters where it cannot.
R03-G-02: Over the past few decades many voluntary organisations have come to manage their volunteers much as firms manage staff. There are role descriptions and application forms, induction sessions, supervisors and annual counts of hours given. The change is usually presented as simple progress. Volunteers who know what is expected of them are said to stay longer, and organisations that can report their hours to funders are better placed to win support. Funders, understandably, prefer measurable outputs, and organisations competing for limited grants have every incentive to supply them. Both claims are plausible, and neither is the whole story. What the managerial model tends to forget is that volunteering was never only a cheaper form of labour. People who give their time without pay are also choosing what to do, with whom and on what terms, and that choice is part of what they value. A retired teacher who helped run a reading club because she liked the children and the other helpers may find, once the club has become a programme with targets and a coordinator, that she has been turned into an unpaid employee of something she no longer recognises. She has lost not her wages, which she never had, but her say. Many such volunteers do not complain; they simply drift away, and their departure is recorded, if at all, as a problem of retention. There is also a quieter loss. Informal associations of volunteers have long been places where people who would never meet at work learn to cooperate, argue and decide things together. A committee that argues for an entire evening over the date of a jumble sale is, among other things, rehearsing the arts of compromise and accountability on which larger institutions depend. When decisions are taken by paid staff and volunteers are slotted into predefined roles, that practice of self-government shrinks. The organisation may deliver its service more reliably while doing less to cultivate the habits that made voluntary life worth defending. None of this is an argument against training or rules as such. A rescue team on a mountain cannot depend on whoever turns up with good intentions, and anyone who works with children ought to be checked. The difficulty arises when standards suited to such demanding tasks are applied across the board, to the allotment society and the neighbourhood library as much as to the lifeboat crew. The sensible question is not whether to professionalise but where, and the answer should depend on what the task requires rather than on what funders find easy to count.
R03-G-03: Few school practices seem as commonsensical as grouping pupils by ability. A teacher facing a class whose members range from those who can barely read to those who devour novels must, it seems, either bore the strong or lose the weak, and sorting children into streams promises to spare her that dilemma. Each group can be taught at its own pace, with material pitched to its level; nobody is held back and nobody is left behind. The argument has the appeal of efficiency, and in a narrow sense it is often right. The trouble lies in what a stream does after it has been formed. Placement usually happens early and rests on tests that measure, along with ability, a child's maturity, her familiarity with the kind of task being set and the amount of help she has had at home. Children who are young for their year are a familiar case: a few months' difference that would be invisible at fifteen can look like a difference of talent at seven. Once placed, however, pupils do not simply learn at different speeds. The lower streams are often given a thinner curriculum, less experienced teachers and quieter expectations, while the upper streams are prepared for examinations the others will never be entered for. The gap that the original test detected is thus widened by the arrangement that was supposed to respond to it, and the later results, which seem to confirm the placement, are partly its product. Defenders of streaming reply that pupils can move between groups, and in principle they can. In practice movement is uncommon, and it is not difficult to see why. A child in a lower stream who has covered less material cannot readily join a group that has covered more, so even a genuine improvement in her understanding may never show up as a change of placement. Teachers, moreover, come to know their pupils as members of a particular set, and the label shapes how her work is read. The door is open, but the corridor behind it grows longer every term. It would be a mistake to conclude that all grouping is harmful. Teaching a class of widely mixed attainment is genuinely demanding, and some arrangements avoid the worst effects of streaming: grouping pupils separately for particular subjects, regrouping them frequently and keeping the curriculum common, so that a move between groups remains a realistic possibility rather than a formal one. What distinguishes these arrangements from the rigid stream is not that they ignore differences in attainment but that they refuse to treat a single early measurement as a verdict.
R03-G-04: When a welfare benefit goes unclaimed by many of the people entitled to it, the usual explanation is that they did not know about it, did not need it badly enough or could not be bothered. The explanation locates the problem in the claimant. It rarely asks what claiming actually involves: discovering that the benefit exists, working out whether one qualifies, gathering documents that may be held by three different offices, completing a form whose questions assume a settled address and a regular income, and then, often, doing it all again a few months later to prove that nothing has changed. These demands are usually described as administrative friction, an unfortunate but neutral by-product of running any large programme. They are not neutral. Every hour required to claim is an hour that some people can spare more easily than others, and the people least able to spare it are frequently those the programme was meant to help: the seriously ill, those working irregular shifts, those for whom scarcity has already consumed much of the attention that form-filling demands. A requirement that costs a comfortable applicant an afternoon may cost a struggling one the benefit itself. There is a further reason to look closely at such burdens. Because they are set through forms, procedures and office hours rather than through legislation, they can change who receives a benefit without any public decision that it should. A government that wished to spend less on a programme but did not wish to say so could add a document to the list or shorten the period for renewal, and the number of recipients would fall while the rules of entitlement stayed exactly as they were. Whether or not anyone intends this, the effect is a form of policy made out of sight, insulated from the debate that a change in the law would provoke. This is not to say that verification is illegitimate. Public programmes depend on the belief that money goes to those entitled to it, and some checking sustains that belief among the taxpayers who fund them. But the costs of checking are borne in two places, in the office and in the lives of applicants, and only the first tends to be counted. A sound design would weigh the time and strain imposed on claimants as seriously as the cost of the errors it prevents, and would treat a large gap between entitlement and receipt as evidence about the system rather than about the people outside it.
R03-G-05: Discussions of social capital commonly distinguish two kinds of tie. Bonding ties link people who are alike in some respect that matters to them, such as kinship, faith, neighbourhood or trade, and they supply loyalty and mutual help. Bridging ties link people across such lines, and they supply information, opportunities and the habit of dealing with strangers. Having drawn the distinction, many writers proceed to rank the two. Bridging is cast as the civic virtue that open societies need; bonding is regarded with suspicion, as the stuff of cliques, favouritism and inward-looking communities. The ranking is attractive partly because it flatters an ideal of openness, and partly because the dangers of tight-knit groups are so easy to picture, whereas their quieter contributions rarely make news. The ranking is too quick. Consider a family that moves to a city where it knows no one except a handful of people from its home district. Those people find it a room, lend it money, explain which offices to visit and which employers pay on time. They are bonding ties in the purest sense, and without them the family might never acquire the stability from which wider contacts become possible. The first job outside the community, or the first friendship with a neighbour of a different background, frequently comes through someone who was met by way of the close circle. In such cases bonding is not the rival of bridging but its precondition. It does not follow that close groups are always benign. The same density of ties that allows a community to support its members allows it to watch them, and the help it offers can come with a demand for conformity: marry within, trade within, think as we do. A young woman who wishes to train for an occupation the group disapproves of may find that the network which once sustained her family now stands in her way, and that the price of leaving it is the loss of everything it provided. Here the closeness that was a resource becomes a closure. What separates the two cases is not the strength of the bonding ties but their permeability: whether membership of the close group is compatible with forming ties outside it, or is made conditional on refusing them. A policy that tried to weaken community networks in the name of integration would therefore risk destroying the very support that allows newcomers to reach beyond those networks in the first place. A better question to ask of any close group is not how tightly it binds but whether it lets its members go.
R03-G-06: Introducing video review into professional sport seemed to settle an old grievance. For as long as games have had officials, players and spectators have complained that decisions were wrong, and now there was a technology that could show, from several angles and at any speed, what had really happened. Few people expected that the result would be a new and more corrosive kind of dispute. Yet that is what many supporters now describe: arguments that once ended with the whistle continue through slow-motion replays, frozen frames and lines drawn on screens, and they seem less settled than before. The puzzle dissolves once we ask what the referee's authority was for. It was never simply a matter of being right. A match needs some means of converting a contested event into a settled fact quickly enough for play to continue, and the referee supplied it by being final. Players accepted decisions they believed mistaken not because they trusted the official's eyesight but because they had accepted, in joining the game, that someone must decide and that the decision would stand. Error was tolerated as the price of finality, and since the errors fell, over a season, on all sides alike, the price seemed bearable. Review alters this bargain in two ways. First, it relocates authority. The decision now seems to belong to the replay, and the referee on the field becomes a provisional judge whose rulings await confirmation from elsewhere. Second, and less obviously, it changes the kind of question being asked. Whether a challenge was reckless, or whether an attacker gained an advantage, is a matter of judgement that a trained official can make in a moment. Whether a toe was ahead of a defender's shoulder at the instant the ball was struck is presented as a matter of fact, yet the answer depends on which frame is chosen and where the line is drawn, choices that the apparent precision of the image conceals. A decision dressed as measurement invites challenge in a way that an acknowledged judgement does not, because every measurement can be disputed by another. None of this is a case for abandoning the cameras. A goal awarded for a shot that plainly missed, or a player sent off for a foul committed by someone else, is an injustice that no appeal to finality can make acceptable, and replays remove such errors cheaply. The mistake lies in treating review as a means of perfecting every marginal call. Confined to clear and obvious errors, it supports the referee's authority; extended to the margins, it dissolves the very finality that made officiating possible.
R03-G-07: Every few years a new survey announces that trust in public institutions has fallen again. Respondents are asked how much confidence they have in parliament, the courts, the police or the press, their answers are averaged, and the declining line is offered as evidence of a crisis. The finding is treated as self-interpreting: less trust is bad, more trust is good, and the task of leaders is to restore it. Each step of that reasoning deserves more scrutiny than it usually receives. Begin with what the question measures. A person asked how far she trusts the courts may be reporting her estimate of their competence, her view of their honesty, her approval of recent verdicts, or simply her mood about public life in general. Answers about quite different institutions tend to rise and fall together, which suggests that much of what is captured is a general disposition rather than a considered judgement about any particular body. Nor does the answer reliably predict conduct. People who tell interviewers that they distrust the courts continue to sign contracts that only courts can enforce, and people who profess little confidence in the health service continue to take the medicines it prescribes. If trust is fundamentally a matter of what we are prepared to rely on, the survey and the behaviour can come apart, and it is not obvious that the survey is the better witness. A second difficulty is that falling trust is ambiguous even where it is real. It may mean that institutions have become less reliable. It may also mean that citizens have come to expect more of them, or that information about their failures, once hidden, now circulates freely. In the last case the decline records not a deterioration in the institution but an improvement in the public's knowledge of it. The philosophical point beneath this is simple and often forgotten: trust is valuable only when it is placed in what is trustworthy. A population that trusted a corrupt police force completely would not be enjoying a civic good; it would be making a mistake, and one that the corrupt would be glad to exploit. What we should want is not high trust but well-calibrated trust, trust that rises and falls with the reliability of its object. This does not license complacency. Distrust, warranted or not, has consequences of its own. Citizens who doubt that taxes are spent honestly may be readier to evade them; communities that expect the police to be indifferent may stop reporting crimes, which in turn makes the police less effective and the distrust more justified. A decline in measured trust can therefore be the beginning of a spiral that no recalibration will halt by itself, because the institution's reliability depends partly on the cooperation that distrust withdraws. The point is not that the numbers are meaningless but that they cannot, on their own, tell us whether we face a failing institution, a better-informed public or a passing mood. What would tell us more is evidence of a different kind: whether expressions of trust track independent measures of institutional performance over time, whether people who say they distrust an institution still rely on it when something important is at stake, and whether trust differs between those who have dealt with an institution directly and those who know it only by reputation. Such evidence is harder to gather than a single question repeated every few years, and it yields no simple line on a chart for commentators to lament. That is precisely its value.
R03-G-08: A familiar story about civic life holds that ordinary people have withdrawn from it. Where their grandparents joined lodges, unions, parents' associations and choral societies, attended meetings and stood for office in them, people today are said to stay at home, absorbed in private amusements and too busy or too distrustful to join anything. The story is usually told as a matter of individual choice and individual failing, and the remedies proposed follow naturally from it: people should be encouraged, shamed or gently nudged back into joining. There is another way to read much of the same evidence. What has declined is not association as such but a particular form of it: the federation of local branches, each with its own officers, meetings and dues, linked through elected delegates to regional and national bodies. In its place, many of the organisations that now claim to speak for citizens are run by professional staff from a central office. They recruit supporters through mailing lists and advertisements, ask them for money rather than time, and consult them, if at all, through surveys. Their membership lists may be long, but a member is someone who has made a payment, not someone who has attended a meeting, and nothing in the organisation's routine requires that members ever meet one another. Read this way, the decline is less a withdrawal from below than a transformation from above. Organisations discovered that it was cheaper and more effective, at least for the purposes of lobbying and publicity, to raise money from many distant supporters than to sustain an expensive structure of local branches with their own halls, officers and opinions. Funders, too, preferred bodies with a clear national voice and a small, accountable staff, and the habits of professional management spread from one organisation to the next. The people who drifted away from the older associations may not have rejected participation at all; they may simply have been offered fewer occasions for it. The distinction matters because the federated association did something its successors do not. It taught people with no political ambitions how to run a meeting, keep minutes, manage a budget, argue for a motion and accept defeat when it was voted down. These were not trivial accomplishments; they were the ordinary apprenticeship of democratic citizenship for many who would never hold public office. It also tied the local to the national: a member in a small town could, through a chain of elected representatives, influence what the national body did. A donor to a professionally managed organisation may support its aims with real conviction, but she learns none of these skills and holds no comparable thread of influence over what is done in her name. It would be easy to turn this into nostalgia, and nostalgia would mislead. Many of the old associations excluded women or people of the wrong background, and their local meetings could be stifling and petty. The new organisations, for their part, have often been more effective at changing laws. Nor have people stopped gathering; they form online groups and informal networks with remarkable ease. But these are seldom built to govern themselves through elected officers and binding votes. If the loss is real, it is the loss of a school of self-government, and it will not be repaired by urging individuals to join more. It would require organisations to find reasons, and funders to give them reasons, to want members who turn up.
